results.summary: This design implements a ring oscillator whose frequency is measured by a 64-bit counter. The counter value is shifted by the cnt_shift inputs and can be stopped or reset. The author measured an oscillation frequency of approximately 504 MHz from the counter output. It was created as a test module for the TT05 power switching FET.

This project chains 128 D flip-flops in series, creating a long shift register. The documentation is minimal and uses vague language, making the exact functionality unclear. It requires two unspecified external devices called 'encabultors' for input and output processing. The design was created in Wokwi and appears to be an educational or test circuit.

This design draws a bouncing ball on a 640x480 VGA display and accepts commands over SPI to set its position and velocity. The ball physics engine updates every six video frames and rebounds off screen edges. It requires a TinyVGA-style PMOD for video output and an SPI master to send commands. The design was tested with a cocotb testbench and includes velocity clamping and reset behavior.

This is an 8-bit processor that communicates with an external FPGA driver over SPI and can animate a 7-segment display. The driver initializes instruction and data memories from .mem files and signals the processor to start execution. After execution, the user can view register contents or watch an animation on the display. The design requires an external FPGA (e.g., Digilent Nexys A7) and optionally a device that supports SPI.

This project generates a 640x480 VGA video signal with a demoscene-style animated background and a central logo inspired by the Tiny Tapeout mark. The image is computed entirely in hardware using combinational logic without any frame buffer or external memory. It requires a VGA PMOD for output and offers optional controls to invert colors or freeze the logo. The design uses reduced-resolution coordinates for a pixelated retro visual style.

This is a 4-bit password security system built with logic gates that grants access for the correct code and triggers a persistent alarm for a trap code (1111). It uses an SR latch to keep the buzzer and red LED on even after inputs change, requiring a manual reset. The design is implemented in Wokwi and uses an 8-position DIP switch, push buttons, LEDs, and a buzzer. It demonstrates combinational and sequential logic for hardware security applications.

This design implements a 1D Kalman filter that fuses accelerometer and gyroscope data from an MPU-6500 IMU to compute Roll and Pitch angles. It uses an SPI master to read the sensor, a CORDIC core for atan2 calculation, and a UART transmitter to output the angles as a binary stream. External hardware required includes an MPU-6500 (or compatible) IMU and a USB-serial adapter for UART reception. The design was tested on a Tiny Tapeout FPGA breakout board.

This is a silicon implementation of Conway's Game of Life on an 8x32 grid with support for MAX7219 LED matrix output. It offers a demo mode with pre-loaded patterns and a manual mode for loading initial states row by row. External hardware required is a MAX7219 LED matrix module (FC-16). Silicon test reports confirm it works, though there is a known bug causing a delay before the demo animation starts.

This is an 8-bit linear feedback shift register (LFSR) that generates pseudo-random numbers. All input and bidirectional pins are unused, and the 8-bit output appears on the output pins. The design is a simple sequential PRNG block written in Verilog. No external hardware or test results are documented.

This design implements a digital-based operational transconductance amplifier (OTA) that requires a 50 kHz clock and two input signals. The output current is proportional to the number of pulses in the output stages. The documentation is sparse and does not specify the exact circuit topology or performance. It was created in Wokwi and appears to be an experimental or educational project.
